title: Omitting Frozen‐Soil Effects in Hydrological Models Introduces Biases in Estimated Runoff Sensitivity to Climate Change in Cold Basins
content:
Abstract

Proper representation of cryospheric processes is essential for accurate hydrological simulation in cold mountainous catchments. Frozen soil, a key cryospheric element, is sometimes overlooked in hydrological models, and its hydrological influence remains insufficiently explored. This study compares two versions of the Tsinghua Representative Elementary Watershed-Tracer-aided model (THREW-T): THREW-FS (with a frozen soil module) and THREW-NoFS (without a frozen soil module), to evaluate runoff-projection biases caused by omitting frozen-soil effects. Results showed: (a) Both models accurately simulated streamflow, but they differed in isotope behavior and subsurface runoff partitioning. THREW-FS estimated a much higher annual subsurface runoff contribution than THREW-NoFS (68.5% vs. 41.3%), providing the process basis for their different runoff sensitivities. (b) Both models estimated decreasing runoff with rising temperatures and increasing runoff with higher precipitation, but THREW-NoFS model showed a higher changing rate. On average, the runoff change estimated by THREW-NoFS was 2.26 times that estimated by THREW-FS in temperature perturbation scenarios and 1.37 times in precipitation perturbation scenarios. (c) Divergences in runoff sensitivity arose from differences in surface-subsurface runoff partitioning and dynamic soil property. THREW-NoFS produced a better water supply condition for evaporation, making it more sensitive to temperature increases than to precipitation increases. These findings suggest that while a model without a frozen soil module can perform well in streamflow simulation, it may overestimate runoff sensitivity to climate perturbations. This study also highlights the value of tracer-aided approach in constraining uncertainties in runoff component partitioning and producing credible runoff projections in cold mountainous basins.
